explanations.answer: The servants who stand in His house
explanations.explanation: Servants, yes. Psalm 135:1-2 says, "Give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD…" Those are the ones being called, and they're already standing in the courts of God's house. Right where it counts.

explanations.answer: The kings who rule the nations
explanations.explanation: Kings do show up in this psalm, but not in the call to praise. In Psalm 135:10-11 they're the ones the LORD struck down, like Sihon and Og. The call in verses 1-2 goes to "servants of the LORD." Nobody's handing out crowns in these two verses.

explanations.answer: The shepherds who watch the flocks
explanations.explanation: Not a single shepherd in this psalm, and not a single sheep either. Psalm 135:1-2 calls the servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God. So the flocks can keep grazing, friend.

True, and it's right there in Psalm 135:3: "Hallelujah, for the LORD is good…" The psalm doesn't make you hunt for the reason. It hands it over in a few short words. Sometimes the best reasons fit on a cookie box lid.

Look again, friend, because Psalm 135:3 says, "Hallelujah, for the LORD is good…" So goodness is the reason, right there in the verse. It's sitting there like a fresh cookie on the cooling rack, waiting for you to grab it. Easy to miss when you're rushing.

Treasured possession is the phrase. Psalm 135:4 says, "For the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession." Treasured is a word I didn't hear much from the back of a junk drawer, so I love it a whole lot.

No army in this verse. Psalm 135:4 says the LORD chose Israel as "His treasured possession." Treasured, not mighty. The psalm saves "great" for the LORD Himself in the next verse: "For I know that the LORD is great…" (Psalm 135:5).

That's a nice phrase, but it isn't the one this psalm uses. Psalm 135:4 says the LORD chose Israel as "His treasured possession." The word "great" comes in the very next verse, and it's about the LORD: "For I know that the LORD is great…" (Psalm 135:5).

Above is the word. Psalm 135:5 says, "For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods." Not level with them, not in their group, but above every one. That's a lot of weight for one tiny word.
Beside sounds close, but it would put the LORD right next to the others, on the same level. Psalm 135:5 says, "our Lord is above all gods." Above is a whole different spot, friend.
Among would put the LORD in the crowd. Psalm 135:5 says, "our Lord is above all gods." Above the whole crowd, not mixed in with it. Different word, different spot entirely.

Not quite, friend. Psalm 135:6 says the LORD does all that pleases Him "in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths." That includes the deep seas, so no spot is off limits. Even the deepest water is on the list.

False, because the deep seas are right there on the list. Psalm 135:6 says the LORD does all that pleases Him "in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths." Heavens, earth, seas, depths, and no corner skipped. Not even the bottom of the ocean gets a "no entry" sign.

True! Psalm 135:7 says He "brings forth the wind from His storehouses." Wind with a storehouse. I can't keep one cookie in my cookie jar past lunch, and He's got whole winds in storage. That's a pretty big stockroom.

That one's sitting right in the verse, friend. Psalm 135:7 says He "brings forth the wind from His storehouses." Storehouses, plural, so there's no shortage of room. Check the verse and you'll find it waiting there.

This verse is a heavy one. Psalm 135:8 says, "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." The psalm names the firstborn, and that's the word to hold onto here. I think it's okay to let a verse like this be heavy for a moment.

Heavy verse, so let's be careful with the words. Psalm 135:8 says He struck down "the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." The psalm says firstborn, not strongest. The verse doesn't mention strength at all.

This one's heavy, so let's get the word right. Psalm 135:8 says He struck down "the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." Firstborn means the first one born, not the youngest. The psalm says firstborn, and I think we hold that one gently.

explanations.answer: Gave it to Israel as an inheritance
explanations.explanation: Inheritance is right. Psalm 135:12 says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." Two words, one gift, and both point to Israel. Most inheritances come with a lawyer and a pile of paperwork, but this verse just says "He gave."

The psalm doesn't leave that land empty. Psalm 135:12 says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." So by the verse's own words, the land had someone to receive it, and that was Israel. Not a vacant lot in sight.

Nothing in this psalm turns that land into a desert. Psalm 135:12 says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." The land goes from those kings to Israel as a gift. No sand, just a handoff.

One generation would be a short run, and the psalm goes way past that. Psalm 135:13 says, "Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations." So it's all generations, not one. One generation is about how long a fresh batch lasts when the family walks in.

False, and the psalm says it big. Psalm 135:13 says, "Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations." Not one generation, not two, but all of them. Grandkids, great-grandkids, great-great-grandkids, and the renown goes right along.

Compassion is the word. Psalm 135:14 says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." Vindicate and compassion in one verse. That's a lot of good news packed into one sentence.

Earlier the psalm does talk about the LORD striking down Egypt and mighty kings in verses 8-11. But verse 14 is about His people and His servants, and there the word is compassion. Psalm 135:14 says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." Compassion, friend.

Contempt isn't in this psalm at all. Psalm 135:14 says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." Compassion is the word the psalm picks for His servants, and I'm glad it does.

People made them, and the psalm says so plainly. Psalm 135:15 says, "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men." Silver and gold, shaped by hands. I stamp cookies all day, and not one of them has ever been put in charge of anything.
The psalm doesn't say that. It says the idols of the nations are "made by the hands of men." (Psalm 135:15) So the makers are people, working with silver and gold.
Angels don't show up anywhere in this psalm. Psalm 135:15 says the idols are "made by the hands of men." Human hands, not a heavenly delivery. Nobody had to wait on a shipment from the sky.
That's the opposite of what the psalm says. Psalm 135:17 says, "they have ears, but cannot hear…" So the ears are there, but the hearing isn't. Ears on the outside and nothing coming through.
False, and that's the right call. Psalm 135:17 says, "they have ears, but cannot hear…" Ears on the outside, hearing nowhere. Even my oven timer does its job.

They become like them. Psalm 135:18 says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." That verse follows the list of what the idols can't do: speak, see, hear, and no breath in their mouths (Psalm 135:16-17). I think that's worth sitting with for a minute.

Riches don't show up in that verse. Psalm 135:18 says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." Silver and gold come up in verse 15, but that's what the idols are made of. What happens to the makers and the trusters is that they become like them.

Long lives aren't mentioned in this psalm. Psalm 135:18 says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." Becoming like them is the thing the verse says happens. I think that's a line to take seriously, friend.
The house of Aaron is right. Psalm 135:19 says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" Israel first, then Aaron, and the calls keep rolling down the line.
Eli isn't named anywhere in this psalm. Psalm 135:19 says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" Aaron is the one named right after Israel.
Zadok isn't named in this psalm either. Psalm 135:19 says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" Of these three names, only Aaron made it into the psalm.

True. Psalm 135:20 says, "O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!" That's four calls in a row across verses 19 and 20: Israel, Aaron, Levi, and those who fear the LORD. Nobody gets to stand in the back with their arms crossed.

Check verse 20 again, friend. It says, "O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!" So right after the house of Levi, the call does go out to those who fear the LORD. That's the fourth call in a row, and it's the last one before the closing blessing.
Jerusalem is it. Psalm 135:21 says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion" and then adds, "He who dwells in Jerusalem." That's the address the psalm gives.
Bethel isn't in this psalm. Psalm 135:21 says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion" and then adds, "He who dwells in Jerusalem." Different address, friend. The last blessing names Jerusalem.

Hebron isn't named anywhere in this psalm. Psalm 135:21 says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion" and then adds, "He who dwells in Jerusalem." The place the psalm gives is Jerusalem, so that's the one to remember.
